items.body: “There are black silences, like thunderclouds, that burst into flashes of music,” H. G. Wells writes in Select Conversations with an Uncle. The phrase finds an almost literal visual counterpart in Jordan Reyes’s cover for Songs for Sad Poets Vol. III: a dense black expanse pressing against a bleached, nearly featureless sky, its uneven boundary resembling storm clouds seen in negative. It also anticipates a pivotal moment in “Sigils of Decay”, when the music comes to such an abrupt halt that, on first hearing, I had to check whether it was still playing. Out of that prolonged absence a low rumble eventually emerges, giving voice to the disquiet that runs through the latest collaboration between Siavash Amini & Eugene Thacker. The three pieces included are dedicated respectively to Vietnamese poet Hàn Mặc Tử, Brazilian Symbolist João da Cruz e Sousa and Austrian poet Nikolaus Lenau, figures connected by the tradition of the poète maudit. “Leprous Doubt”, for Hàn Mặc Tử, opens with dissonant textures, degraded sounds and sudden changes of register. It is unsettling and unsettled, meandering in unforeseen directions and making its discomfort palpable. The music pauses and resumes, pitching antagonistic forces against one another; moments of sweeping grandeur coexist with passages of intimate travail. It repeatedly attempts to steady itself before faltering again. Circular tones eventually lift to reveal the “glowing abyss” of Thacker’s poem, while intensifying drones recede until a solitary, quivering tone remains. “Sigils of Decay”, for Cruz e Sousa, pushes this instability into silence itself. The long interruption at its centre makes the eventual return of sound unusually physical. As the low frequencies slowly reassert themselves, muted fragments accumulate into a dark, suspended mass. Thacker writes of “muted music / woven by / night spiders”, an image that seems uncannily close to what Amini constructs: strands of sound gradually spun into a crepuscular firmament of drones and disarticulated fragments, only to loosen again. The connection with Cruz e Sousa is equally suggestive. His poetry transforms an inexplicable melancholy into a confrontation with the Infinite; Thacker condenses that metaphysical sadness into the colder “Dread of / Infinite space. / Dread of / Distant skies.” At nineteen minutes, “Dead Eyes, Dark Stars” is the album’s most expansive piece. Its opening is nocturnal, with celestial voices suspended above slumbering coils of sound. These gradually precipitate into increasingly abrasive textures, yet the music pulls itself back towards a softer harmonic balance. Timbral shifts become more pronounced as the underlying material turns metallic and resonant. Lenau’s recurring world of night, forests, barren landscapes, grief and death finds an oblique counterpart here: the landscape seems to have been emptied of narrative and retained as atmosphere, shadow and distant light. Voice assumes a much greater presence than on the first Songs for Sad Poets, although words never present themselves as intelligible text. Synthetic voices gather into spectral choirs and dissolve into the surrounding music, allowing Thacker’s poems to remain embedded within the pieces without requiring the listener to follow them line by line. The relationship between poetry and sound consequently operates through images, structures and emotional pressure: Hàn Mặc Tử’s diseased bodies and impossible skies, Cruz e Sousa’s metaphysical melancholy, Lenau’s nocturnal desolation. Each piece finally leaves a coda of silence. By then, Reyes’s cover feels increasingly inseparable from the music: darkness occupies most of the field, while its opposite persists beyond its ragged edge. H.G. Wells’s “black silences” provide an apt description of an album where silence continually threatens to swallow the music, yet also provides the space from which it can begin again. To lift the veil on the production process we have spoken directly to Saivash Amini. On the first Songs for Sad Poets, Eugene Thacker’s poems were never actually spoken; the words were translated into sound without becoming voice. On Vol. III, you take almost the opposite route, programming voice-synthesis software to perform the poems and then processing as many as forty voices until language becomes unintelligible. What interested you in bringing the human voice into the project only to erase its legibility again? Do you still think of these pieces as songs, or has the distinction between voice, text and sound become irrelevant? The idea of voice synthesis came out of a conversation with Eugene about his dislike of the human voice and the vocal music he actually liked like Ligeti’s requiem, where micropolyphony, among other techniques, were used to mask the intelligibility of the text and transform the human choir into something entirely different. I have much of the liberty of a large choir in my DAW with voice synthesis software. It’s not actually a human voice, so I can make a sound very modulated and affected when singing. And I can have as many as I want to have, as long as my CPU can handle it, so micropolyphony can be much more extreme and differently intricate. And yes, I do think of these as songs, they are structured around the poem. Just not conventional songs with known musical structures. But that’s when I’m making them. There’s no point trying to find the points of reference to poems if you’re just listening, they are trying to convey the same thing. Listening closely to the three pieces, decay seems to function as a compositional process rather than simply as an atmosphere. “Leprous Doubt” repeatedly loses substance and regains it; “Sigils of Decay” moves through accumulation and withdrawal; and the nineteen-minute “Dead Eyes, Dark Stars” forms large masses of sound that gradually weather away, return and finally disappear. This concern with appearance, erosion and reconstitution also seems connected to Eidolon, Caligo and Severed Like the Red Moon, where sounds are made to float, bleed, collapse, be mutilated and reassembled. Has this become a central way for you to think about musical form? Yes and no, I have been more and more putting focus in making structures and out evolving and directional textures made out of different approaches to generating harmony. It’s not all I think about when making pieces but more likely the result of intentional putting together of smaller directional elements of different duration. So the micro is what determines the macro, and a lot of the times I’m thinking of micro. The poets invoked on Vol. III come from very different linguistic and cultural histories: Hàn Mặc Tử and Vietnam’s “Chaos” school, João da Cruz e Sousa and Brazilian Symbolism, and Nikolaus Lenau and the tradition of Weltschmerz. How did you and Eugene Thacker arrive at these particular figures, and what drew you to bringing such different poetic traditions together within the same musical cycle? That’s all Eugene’s side of the project but the thread that links them all is in the Poet Maudit term which the title comes from. They all fit that category. Much of your recent work has begun from literary or historical material: Ibn Sina on eremos, Xavier Villaurrutia on The Sweat of Earth, early Iranian piano recordings and Malakoot on Caligo, as well as Houshang Golshiri on Severed Like the Red Moon. In each case, the source seems to act less as something to illustrate than as a force that changes the way you treat sound. What does literature give you that a purely musical starting point does not, and has worked so closely with Eugene Thacker altered the way you now read a text as a composer? Using literature for my work goes to my first album. Then I have three collaborations with Matt Finney which were based on his reading his poems and sending them to me. Serus had a strong relationship with the writings of Blanchot I can go on… I find using literature gives me a structure and image which I can turn into sound worlds. I can imagine something to convey that image. I find that very exciting but a lot of background work before the project starts is done on purely musical material. Working with Eugene changed my workflow in general and made my relationship with literature deeper than it was before, and it gave me a lot to think about when it comes to making sound that conveys what one word is telling me. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.album: Anushka Chkheidze + Robert Lippok :: The Sky Was Out of Tune (Morr Music)
items.excerpt: Natural recordings, soft rhythms, distortion, metallic noises, melody, and digital artifacts continually lean against one another without settling. By the end it feels less like eight compositions and more like half an hour spent inside a system that was continuously adjusting itself while you were listening, and never quite finished. Everything feels connected by residue The Sky Was Out of Tune by Anushka Chkheidze + Robert Lippok   Anushka Chkheidze and Robert Lippok make sense together.
items.body: Natural recordings, soft rhythms, distortion, metallic noises, melody, and digital artifacts continually lean against one another without settling. By the end it feels less like eight compositions and more like half an hour spent inside a system that was continuously adjusting itself while you were listening, and never quite finished. Everything feels connected by residue The Sky Was Out of Tune by Anushka Chkheidze + Robert Lippok   Anushka Chkheidze and Robert Lippok make sense together. Chkheidze is a Georgian composer and producer based in the Netherlands. Lippok is Berlin, To Rococo Rot, Raster Noton, installation work, decades of treating electronic sound as material that gets layered, cut, reshaped, and left partially unresolved. They met in Tbilisi in 2019 through a workshop program, worked together on Glacier Music II, then built that into Uncontrollable Thoughts, their first joint album for Morr Music in 2025. Morr Music has spent decades in that specific space between electronica, ambient, post-rock, and minimal composition—múm, The Notwist, B. Fleischmann, music where texture and atmosphere carry as much weight as conventional structure. A natural home for this collaboration. The Sky Was Out of Tune pushes further. Eight pieces, titled only with Roman numerals, and they really don’t function as separate tracks so much as sections of one continuous object. That makes sense, the music grew out of a live performance at Berlin’s Neue Nationalgalerie. Everything feels connected by residue. A texture disappears and something remains behind it. A rhythmic idea dissolves into ambience. A metallic sound becomes the thing guiding the next section without announcing itself as such. “I” opens with what sounds like field recording, natural ambience, small bell-like tones, rattling, paper movement, objects handled close to a microphone. Hard to identify exactly what some of those sounds are. Records that begin this way can immediately position themselves as documentary field recording works where the environment becomes the subject. Here the material behaves differently. It’s preparation. Those sounds establish a physical space before synthetic material gets pushed into it. Tiny rhythmic impulses sit beneath the surface :: That becomes one of the strongest ideas running through the record. Chkheidze and Lippok are extremely good at preparing the listener for something before revealing what it is. Ambience gathers density. Distortion arrives gradually. Tiny rhythmic impulses sit beneath the surface before becoming clearer. Metallic sounds enter and disappear like objects moving through the stereo field. No obvious drops. No resolutions. They build toward changes in texture instead, which is a harder thing to make feel earned. Their process on Uncontrollable Thoughts involved long improvisations, selecting ideas afterward, sending projects between one another. Chkheidze contributing drums, piano, vocals. Lippok adding noise, harmony, sometimes reshaping the entire piece. He’s described his production as primarily layering, constructing, collaging, not sitting at a keyboard writing chord progressions. You can hear that philosophy all over this record. Compared to Uncontrollable Thoughts, The Sky Was Out of Tune is more dissolved. The previous album still had recognizable individual pieces—”Bird Song,” “Rainbow Road,” soft beats, organ drones, clear rhythmic personalities moving between tracks. Boundaries here have almost completely disappeared. Uncontrollable Thoughts felt like two musicians improvising compositions. This feels like those same two musicians improvising an environment. The rhythm is still present but behaves more like weather than percussion. Digital texture and ambience overlapping :: Soft electro rhythms surface throughout, especially when the album settles into its more defined sections. Nothing becomes overly forceful. Even when distortion enters it feels incorporated into the ambience rather than placed over it. There are moments that recall the softer edges of early Mille Plateaux material, digital texture and ambience overlapping until it becomes difficult to decide which one you’re actually listening to. The late 90s and early 2000s electronica sensibility is present throughout, that specific understanding that small rhythmic gestures can carry enormous emotional weight if given room. “VII” is the most interesting section on the record and it lasts 35 seconds. The glitches become more exposed, textures start colliding, and suddenly the album sounds like it might move somewhere completely different—like a corrupted transitional file that accidentally became part of the release. Its short duration is what gives it impact. “VII” functions as a doorway into “VIII” rather than a standalone piece. An introduction to the outro. And that tiny moment reveals something about the whole record, Chkheidze and Lippok are comfortable letting an idea exist only as long as it needs to. A texture doesn’t have to develop into a full track. A rhythmic pattern can appear for seconds and disappear. Something can sound important and still never return. The title describes the music unusually well. A sky being out of tune doesn’t mean the environment has collapsed, it means something familiar has shifted slightly enough that you start paying closer attention. That’s what happens here. Natural recordings, soft rhythms, distortion, metallic noises, melody, and digital artifacts continually lean against one another without settling. By the end it feels less like eight compositions and more like half an hour spent inside a system that was continuously adjusting itself while you were listening, and never quite finished. The Sky Was Out of Tune is available on Morr Music. items.body: Landscape 07 unfolds in breaths: slow waves advance, overlap, recede and return in subtly altered forms. The movement is continuous, yet it can escape a distracted listener. You need to stop, allow the piece to find its own pace and follow its changes as you might follow shadows moving across a field. An accomplished expression of stillness, physical presence and transformation landscape 07 by fields we found / quiet details   Fields We Found is the alias of British musician, mastering engineer and visual artist Alex Gold, who founded the quiet details label in 2023. Following releases on Home Normal, Seil Records, handstitched*, and Ambientologist, Gold has increasingly focused his work on extended listening. The Landscape series grew out of compositions created for his personal meditation practice; over time, the creative process itself also became a form of meditation. Landscape 07, the seventh installment in the series, runs for more than twenty-five minutes. It is an extended live performance constructed from electronic instruments, tape and successive layers of sound. The piece begins almost without a threshold. A broad sound emerges from the haze, already inhabited by tremors, gentle fluctuations and distant trails. During the opening minutes, the music gains weight; the volume rises calmly and glimmers of light move across its surface. From here, Landscape 07 unfolds in breaths: slow waves advance, overlap, recede and return in subtly altered forms. The movement is continuous, yet it can escape a distracted listener. You need to stop, allow the piece to find its own pace and follow its changes as you might follow shadows moving across a field. “Later, individual lines drift apart and the landscape opens out. This is where the title finds its true meaning. The horizon remains; the light changes. It is a slow transformation, free of spectacular gestures, shaped by passages that can be felt before they can be defined.” ~Mirco Salvadori The presence of tape can be felt in the sound’s internal movement. The notes have porous edges, slight instabilities and a warmth far removed from artificial stillness. Even when everything appears motionless, something continues to shift. The overall balance gradually changes, brighter colours surface and the mass of sound seems to lift. Later, individual lines drift apart and the landscape opens out. This is where the title finds its true meaning. The horizon remains; the light changes. It is a slow transformation, free of spectacular gestures, shaped by passages that can be felt before they can be defined. Gold handles duration with patience and restraint. Each event is allowed to remain long enough to alter our perception of everything around it. In its central section, the piece takes on a darker, more introspective colour. Threads and reflections continue to move through the texture; through headphones, they reveal small lateral movements, like currents. Light then returns gradually and the music expands without losing its composure. This leads to the point of greatest emotional intensity, reached through patient accumulation. The journey feels natural, almost as though it had formed by itself, while retaining the freedom of a gesture made in the moment. The piece asks for a simple kind of openness: to remain, to listen, to give each nuance time to reveal itself and to accept that the inner landscape may change alongside the sonic one. In these passages, distant echoes of German electronic music from the early 1970s begin to surface. The more abstract expanses of Tangerine Dream’s Zeit, the cosmic materiality of early Klaus Schulze and some of Cluster’s suspended atmospheres come to mind in the way timbre becomes form. Fields We Found keeps everything on an intimate, tactile scale. The connection lies in the trust placed in machines, in their natural drift and in the time a sound needs to reveal its hidden folds. Recording the performance directly to tape preserves the element of risk that gives life to such a gradual process. “A single sound remains, along with tape hiss and a few distant reflections; eventually, these elements also slip beneath the threshold of perception.” ~Mirco Salvadori An even closer affinity leads to Éliane Radigue. Landscape 07 shares the French composer’s attentiveness to what can emerge from within a prolonged sound and to the variations that appear when the ear stops searching for a melody. The historical and poetic distance remains clear; the surface here is denser and more explicitly ambient. Yet the kind of listening it requires is close to Radigue’s: focused, patient and ready to recognise an event within apparent stillness. Pauline Oliveros’ Deep Listening also comes to mind, particularly in its understanding of attention as an active part of the work, as does Suzanne Ciani, in the gentle way electronic sound can suggest physical movement. Towards the end, the piece begins to subtract. The pressure recedes, its lines grow sparse and what remains reveals its irregularities more clearly. The farewell becomes fragile. The long fade avoids any emphatic sense of closure. A single sound remains, along with tape hiss and a few distant reflections; eventually, these elements also slip beneath the threshold of perception. It is an ending fully consistent with the work as a whole: the ear is left to measure the disappearance, while the silence that follows seems to last a little longer. Landscape 07 succeeds because its calmness contains tension. Meditation here has density, pressure and material memory. The instruments breathe, the tapes impart instability and depth, and the studio work preserves the spontaneity of the performance. With each new listen, the hierarchy of details changes: something that first seemed marginal becomes a guide, a fluctuation turns into rhythm, a blur acquires definition. This is music that entrusts its richness to time and draws its strength from time in return. A remarkable entry in the series, and perhaps its most accomplished expression of stillness, physical presence and transformation. Landscape 07 is available on quiet details. items.body: A mesmerizing collision of ambient, jazz, electronics and ritualistic textures, this album unfolds like a deep-space journey that never loses its human pulse. Trumpet drifts through electronic vastness Fade In Brighter Age by Pulsar + Demetrio Cecchitelli   Mahorka has a busy schedule and quite an enormous back catalog, covering various electronic music, from ambient to dub, noise and radically experimental. Confirmed sound artists meet new promising ones in the course of indie, challenging music with no regard for major commercial tendencies. I’ve never heard of Pulsar (Leonardo Pucci) before, but I must say he perfectly teams up with Demitrio Cecchitelli. I’m more familiar with the work of Cecchitelli, notably with the sumptuous Empetus (published years ago by Midira). The addition of trumpet player Jacopo Buda to the soundscapes gives an enriched musical meaning to the album, playing the card of instrumental ambient music with partly experimental-jazzy tones and expansive improvs which evolve on dynamic electronic textures. What we can listen to here is nothing less than a furiously enthralling and original musical trip which starts masterfully with the ethno-ritual and spaced-out “Cosmic Dream”. Such a gorgeous piece with its perpetual circular rhythms covered by inspiring and gently minimal trumpet melodic shifts. It is meticulously crafted without being purely ambient, as it conjugates a vast array of influences, from Buddhist-Zen musical attributes to early minimalism and atmospheric, then bassy, chilled-out vibes. It suggests immensity and nature-like vastness, with its colorful timbres resonating in divine harmony. It is a sprawling track with a magnificent development, always suspenseful, melodically ethereal and dynamic. The second track (“Expanding Light”) also operates a nice syncretism and musical dialogue between acoustic ingredients, wind instruments and electronics, but here we enter a more downtempo, softly moving ambience, less lyrical and tripped-out but equally good and perfectly elaborated. The title track (“Fade in Brighter Age”) almost provides a softly moving dream-pop quality, built on guitars, vibrant chords and slowly enveloping wind sequences, largely embracing a lonesome path and a feeling of consciousness at night. All in all, a varied and semi-jazzy atmospheric ambient album with a flowing cinematic edge. Absolutely recommended and easily one of my personal favorites of this year. For fans of John Hassell, Harold Budd, Peter Knight, Loscil, Bersanin Quartett, Nala Sinephro, and Floating Points. Fade In Brighter Age is available on Mahorka. items.body: Irezumi returns with a deeply immersive ambient journey where granular textures, subtle electronic details, and melancholic atmospheres unfold into a beautifully restrained world of sound. Deeply introspective sound waves flowing all around the room   Irezumi is a French-based abstract-minimal ambient music project formed by sound artist Manuel Mesdag back in 2008. His first album, titled Endurance, is highly regarded by passionate listeners in search of beautifully/carefully designed soundscapes where electronic scintillations meet cinematic expressiveness and instrumental repetitiveness. The project has a Japanese name, which reflects its very own musical signature, turned toward inner worlds and ritualistic passages to a state of deep quietness. Irezumi has been highly productive throughout the years, constantly delivering expressive layered soundtracks imbued with a particular flowing meditative mood. This new album makes no exception and reveals a refined body of calm, enchanting, soothing, and sometimes sorrowful granular synthesized textures, augmented by sparse micro-noises and a palette of sonic effects. A track such as “Deliverance” delivers a progressively enveloping and grainy sonic ambient splendor, passing from very quiet to fully opened sounds. The general mood is very evocative, suggesting something at once tense and darkly opaque, yet infused with lighter emotional vibes. Every piece is built on delicate, fragile, spacious, and deeply introspective sound waves flowing all around the room. Among my favorite moments offered by the album, I can mention the ghostly, blurred-out section of the profoundly melancholic “Unstable” or the trippy, mind-travelling and minimal “Shelter”. Perfect accompaniment for moments of self-reliance and easily recommended for fans of ambient electronica with an impressionistic feeling and tasty, minimal-melodiously inclined acoustic sounds. Never disappoints and is of solid musical value. The album is delivered in beautiful vinyl format and distributed by Paris-based indie label Brique Rouge, known for embracing and promoting a vast range of electronic music, with a particular interest in clubbing, house, and techno music. items.body: What began as an ordinary box of records arriving at work quickly turns into a strange trip down the rabbit hole of Synaptic Cliffs—a label where extraterrestrials, electronic music legends, immaculate vinyl and one very elusive artist called pdqb somehow all make perfect sense.   The box that changed everything “Robert, there’s a box there for you.”“Thanks. I’ll grab it on the way back.” I generally have records delivered to work. Living in Spain, a lesson worth learning quickly is to avoid the post-office unless you have some nostalgia for Soviet Union like queues. “Robert, don’t forget that box.”“No, I’ll be back down.”“Why don’t you take it up with you, out of the way then.”“Right.” Searing Summer heat means that certain jobs, such as carrying boxes up and down flights of stairs, are to be done in one’s own time. But, for some reason, the downstairs gang wanted this box out of sight and out of mind. A nondescript box. Heavy with records, innocent nonetheless. Name. Address of sender. All run of the mill. Perhaps it was the contents; that somehow the sender’s supernatural aura had seeped out from its cardboard cage and given the secretarial staff the heebie-jeebies. Inside, the world of Synaptic Cliffs. Although the return address reads Sascha Dornhöfer, there’s a sense that Pandora herself has put this collection of records together. Nothing chaotic, something mysterious, mystical and bordering on magical. Speaking with Dornhöfer is easy, a pleasure. Pinning down the central artist of Synaptic Cliffs, pdqb, is a story like few others. “pdqb is essentially a character – or maybe something else entirely” So, you are pdqb? Yes, no and maybe. “pdqb is an extraterrestrial who is 127 years old,” and it appears Dornhöfer is “currently possessed by it.” So, you are? “Maybe I’ve only been making music for a few years. Maybe I’ve actually been making music for 30 years. Maybe I’ve already been known under another name. Maybe I’ve been a major producer for other artists. Nobody knows, and nobody is going to find out – at least not through me.” Can you catch heebie-jeebies? This is the story, and Synaptic Cliffs is full of stories. Dornhöfer won’t be held to facts about who he is “because ultimately, this is supposed to be about the music. I don’t want the music to be reduced to a person, a biography, or a recognizable identity. And if people do try to connect everything to a person, then I’d rather give them something so completely absurd that nobody can really make sense of it.” And through the looking glass we go. The label’s style is as difficult to define as its founder. Essentially, the epicentres of this multiverse are pdqb and Perzeptiverdampfkesselqualmtbesinnlich. “pdqb is the main act, mostly electro, but also disco and techno. Perzeptiverdampfkesselqualmtbesinnlich is basically everything else: ambient, experimental stuff, post-punk, scores, soundscapes, that kind of thing.” Ambition is mixed in with the abstract. Opening its doors in 2024, Synaptic Cliffs is now clocking thirty releases across all media with a clear focus on vinyl. Terra firma. Solid ground can also be found when it comes to the connections that pdqb’s music has made with other artists. Legowelt was drafted in for two stellar remixes on the inaugural release Wet Dreams of Jesus Christ with the electro, sci-fi warmth of the original dipped in the delightful haze of Wolfer’s machines. And the names keep coming. Alva Noto, Rolando of Underground Resistance fame, Egyptian Lover, Felix Da Housecat, Umwelt and Roman Flügel with a show-stopping take of “Senftgurken-Prämenöde.” There are also collaborations, the Diskmind EP with Scape One, Guilty Pleasures featuring DMX Krew. And the names keep coming. Reimaginings by Dopplereffekt on Sermons of the Electrofying Messiah. 8½ Bit Replays, a chirpy remix album of the stunning chiptune frolics of 8½ Bit, brings together modern electro masters like PRZ, Galaxian, CEM3340, Dark Vektor and Mesak. New collaborations are on the horizon. Orlando Voorn, Heinrich Dressel and most recently with Edward Ka-Spel, the singer of the Legendary Pink Dots. And… breathe. Where were we? Right, ascending Synaptic Cliffs. “The original compositions are, of course, primarily aimed at the headphone connoisseur listening at home. The remixers are then, so to speak, responsible for the club side of things – although they’re never explicitly commissioned to make something club-friendly. Everyone gets more or less full artistic control. Just like Egyptian Lover, Felix Da Housecat, they can do whatever they want with the track. Of course, you discuss things with each other, but that’s basically how it works.” Just as intriguing as the audio is the visual. The records are beautifully produced, the audio quality singing from the grooves. Art is central. Elaborate swirls and speckled patterns adorn coloured vinyl with sleeves printed to superb quality. And, just like the music, collaborations abound. CONTACT IMMINENT by pdqb & Extrawelt   “Most of them are seriously high-profile artists, people like Maurizio Cattelan (he did the taped banana, an artwork which sold for millions), and Adam Pendleton, and I somehow manage to convince them to get involved” My semi-formed journalistic instincts begin to twitch. Extraterrestrial entities, ok. Million dollar earning modern artists. Hhhmmm?? “By the way, Diskmind (Scape One‘s Quantum Mechanics) was played at Dior’s Spring/Summer Haute Couture show in Paris this year, which made us incredibly happy, because it fit the show perfectly. I’m also a huge fan of Jonathan Anderson.” Wait, maybe my colleagues were on to something. What has this box pulled me into? Fantastical? Supernatural? Whatever this story is, this label, it is definitely one of a kind. Searching for a handrail, let’s get back to the music. “We see ourselves as a premium label. That means no cutting corners anywhere. We work with the best mastering engineers, the records are pressed to the highest possible standards, and the artwork is treated with the same level of care. Everything is done properly.” This is undeniable. But there is also a serious sense of fun to these proceedings. A tongue-in-cheek playfulness that seems to have been lost with the stony-faced seriousness of electronic music or the financial strains of running a label. Dornhöfer is a storyteller, a raconteur who playfully leans into the mysterious with the mischievousness of a boy. The narrative he has woven around Synaptic Cliffs is ever evolving, ever shifting as the imagined somehow takes form.  And that form is very exciting. A label led by a character of boundless energy, an imprint without boundaries, a platform to connect artists and bisect time and space.“I feel another pdqb attack coming……over and out…” Visit https://synapticcliffs.bandcamp.com Cold Calling on the Spirit Line by Perzeptiverdampfkesselqualmtbesinnlich & Edward Ka-SpelThe post Interstellar Seance :: Synaptic Cliffs first appeared on Igloo Magazine.

items.body: Review by Hector Enrique — Throughout his career, Jon Anderson has not limited himself to the paths of progressive rock. His constant exploration of diverse musical languages - in search of new textures and nuances and free from conventional constraints - has led him to expand his sonic palette and reflect it in musical works of very different natures. "The More You Know" (1998), his twelfth studio album, is one of those works that strays furthest from the genre that made Yes one of its leading standard-bearers.Prioritizing gentle, melodic structures over any display of instrumental virtuosity, "The More You Know" moves, almost effortlessly, through pop and world music sounds, in which the arrangements and programming form the foundation upon which much of the album rests. Songs like "Magic Love," "Say Jocky," and "Take, Take, Take" are easy on the ears but don't seem to offer anything substantial. On the other hand, when the English singer's more spiritual side comes to the fore, some of the album's best moments emerge, including the melancholic "Heaven's Love" and "Sad," and the jubilant "Youth" with its ethnic overtones.Also noteworthy are the arrangements on "Dancing Fool" and the light soul-jazz of "Free (Some Would Say)," underpinned by the deep, expressive bass of Bobby Jocky, brother of Francis Jocky, who contributes on keyboards and as a composer. The rest of the album hovers in an accessible average that never quite takes off, with the standout feature being Anderson's angelic voice, which is in fine form. That's no small thing, but it's not enough to overcome a production that, at times, feels overly polished.2/2.5 stars

items.body: Review by A Crimson Mellotron — Finnish band Von Hertzen Brothers released their fifth studio album 'Nine Lives' in 2013 throughUniversal, having previously caught the attention of the press with the records 'Love Remains theSame' and 'Stars Aligned'. This quintet plays an interesting crossover of pop, prog, and folk,offering an eclectic yet accessible type of rock music that definitely has commercial potential butdoes not shy away from unconventional arrangements. The album 'Nine Lives' in particular issubjected to a high-energy, buzzing start, in the face of melodic numbers like 'Insomniac' and'Flowers and Rust', while its ending resorts to mellower, more atmospheric tones that are exploredon the longer songs 'World Without' and 'Prospect for Escape'. Certain instrumental sections are waytoo loud in the recording, especially in the faster tracks in the beginning, but I think thisproblem is taken care of in the second half of the recording. The vocals are fine, but some of thelyrics feel corny, while the album itself strikes you as almost too eclectic, which is probably whatVHB had wanted to do, but this aspect of it may disengage some listeners. I think the main issuewith 'Nine Lives' is the fact that there are very few highlights present. The record is quite solidoverall and the variety of styles covered provides for an engaging listen, but the songs featured onit are mostly hit or miss.

items.body: Darkmechanic released the album “Hypercontrol” on 2 October 2026 through the Slovak label Aliens Production. The eight-track record is the industrial electronic project’s second album and its first release for the label. Alexander Borsov, who records as Darkmechanic, wrote, produced and mastered all eight tracks. “Hypercontrol” comprises: The deceitful idol Puppet Gloomy lake Cau the night cult Hypercontrol Go all….F Resolving a controversy Halloween (Bonus track) Aliens Production describes the album as “a mechanical colossus of industrial energy and electronic flashes.” “Hypercontrol” is available as a digital album on Bandcamp. Aliens Production is a Slovak dark electronics label operating since 1997. Side-Line has previously covered Aliens Production releases by the Polish electro/EBM act Fractal, including “Antidote” in 2023 and “Hide in the light” in 2026, both on the same label. Hypercontrol by Darkmechanic About Darkmechanic Darkmechanic is the solo industrial electronic project of Alexander Borsov, who also records as Dark The Keeper and Stellar Dynamics. The project’s first recorded appearance was a track on the compilation “Dark Virus X-Mas”, released by Russian Dark Community in 2020. Darkmechanic’s debut album, “Ghost Reflection”, followed in 2021, also through Russian Dark Community. Between albums, Borsov contributed remixes to other artists’ releases: “Blood For Blood Remixes” (2023) on DSBP, “Monolith” (2023) by Reagent, “Mvrtyr” (2024) by G.G.F.H. and “Lost EP” (2025) by Synaptic Defect. Darkmechanic also appeared on the compilation “Cyclone Front: Movements and Currents” in 2025. “Hypercontrol”, released on 2 October 2026, is Darkmechanic’s second album and the project’s first release through Aliens Production, five years after “Ghost Reflection”.

The track’s chorus alternates “Han-bun, han-bun, han-bun-bun” (“half, half, half-half”) in Japanese with the English line “Half of me is still asleep.” Each verse plays out as a short back-and-forth: an unfamiliar key in the mailbox, a letter on the fridge that reads only “sorry,” and questions about a name, the time, and whether to go home. The video was uploaded to the duo’s own YouTube channel, @crydopeofficial. “Dark Dopamine” streams on Spotify, Apple Music and other platforms. About Cry DOPE Cry DOPE is the Tokyo-based duo of Syuri and Sonar. The band describes its sound as music that “sits somewhere between a late-night room and the city outside,” sung in both Japanese and English. “Dark Dopamine,” released October 2, 2026, is the duo’s debut single.

items.body: Magic Wands released the single “Guardians” on October 2, 2026 through Metropolis Records. The Los Angeles dream-pop duo of vocalists and guitarists Dexy and Chris Valentine describe the track as a look back at a period that no longer feels real: “This is a song about looking back on a time in your life that doesn’t feel real anymore, even though it really happened.” “Guardians” is the second track lifted from “Sun Kiss,” a new Magic Wands album due in early 2027. It follows “Diamond Rain”, issued in mid-August, which was the first single from the same record. Guardians by Magic Wands “Guardians” is available as a digital single on Bandcamp. Magic Wands’ 2026 singles and EPs “Guardians” and “Diamond Rain” extend a run of releases that started with “Cascades,” the album Magic Wands issued on October 24, 2025. The duo opened 2026 with “Sacred Mirrors,” a January collaboration with Psychedelic Furs guitarist John Ashton. The six-track “Wishing Well” EP followed in April, and Side-Line reviewed it that August. A six-track “Remixes” EP reworking songs from “Cascades” followed in June. Magic Wands remixed Peter Murphy’s “Swoon” in late spring, and Side-Line covered that single when Peter Murphy released “Swoon (Magic Wands Remix)” on May 29, 2026. About Magic Wands Magic Wands formed in Nashville, Tennessee, in the summer of 2008 around vocalists and guitarists Dexy Valentine and Chris Valentine, who began writing together after Dexy moved from Los Angeles to Nashville. The duo later relocated to Los Angeles, where they are now based. Their sound blends dream-pop with shoegaze, post-punk and goth textures, carried by layered guitars, droning synths and Dexy’s vocals. The band debuted with the album “Aloha Moon” (Bright Antenna, 2012), preceded by the EP “Magic Love & Dreams” (2009). “Jupiter” followed on Cleopatra Records in 2016, and “Abrakadabra” on Etxe Records & Productions / Casa del Puente Discos in 2018. Magic Wands self-released “Illuminate” in 2020, then signed to Metropolis Records for “Switch,” released May 12, 2023. Side-Line reviewed “Switch” that September, having already covered the duo’s single “Fortune” in April 2022, the single “Time” that May, and the remix album and tour announced that August. Magic Wands’ sixth album, “Cascades,” arrived in October 2025 and set off the run of singles, remixes and EPs that continued through 2026. “Guardians” now carries that chronology into “Sun Kiss,” the duo’s next album, scheduled for early 2027.

items.body: German electro-industrial project Forma Tadre’s 1996 debut album “Navigator” is available on vinyl for the first time, as the opening release on the new label Analog Frontier. This 30th Anniversary Edition is a 2xLP gatefold pressed on 160g Electric Seaglass Blue vinyl, limited to 300 copies, and is sold through Analog Frontier’s Bandcamp page alongside a digital edition. Analog Frontier describes itself as a label dedicated to pressing CD and digital-only albums to vinyl for the first time, and “Navigator” is its debut release. The gatefold carries entirely new artwork built from period polar-expedition photography. The images include work by Herbert G. Ponting, official photographer of the British Antarctic (“Terra Nova”) expedition led by Robert Falcon Scott. The package also includes a double-sided insert with the album’s full lyrics. Side D of the vinyl edition adds two tracks that have never been released before: “First Land,” recorded in 1995, and “No Gene For Fate,” from 1997. Both date from the “Navigator” era of Forma Tadre’s catalogue. The 13-track edition runs: “Navigator (Part One)” “FX on a Human Subject” “Plasmasleep” “Date Unknown” “Navigator (Part Two)” “Serpent Charmer” “Looking Glass Men” “Mesozoic Tree Ferns” “Gates” “Celebrate the Cult” “Navigator (Part Three)” “First Land” “No Gene For Fate” “Navigator” was written, produced and mixed by Andreas Meyer, the sole member of Forma Tadre. Andreas Torkler handled mastering for the original eleven tracks. Meyer mastered “First Land” and “No Gene For Fate” himself, and Steve Eagle did additional mastering for the vinyl cut. B.A. Donahoo designed the new gatefold artwork, with additional art elements by Jared Cote and Steve Eagle. Hansjoerg Schifferer plays guitar on “Serpent Charmer” and “Celebrate the Cult.” The lacquer was cut at Complete Mastering and the vinyl pressed at Onyx Record Press. Originally released in 1996 on the German label Off Beat, “Navigator” was Meyer’s first release as the sole member of Forma Tadre. The album departed stylistically from the project’s earlier three-piece incarnation. “Navigator” centers on a theme of exploration and combines symphonic instrumental passages with EBM tracks. Meyer’s interest in the occult and in H.P. Lovecraft informed tracks including “Date Unknown,” “Celebrate the Cult,” “Gates” and “Mesozoic Tree Ferns.” The 30th Anniversary Edition is available as a digital album and as the limited vinyl edition on Bandcamp. Shipping of physical copies to the EU is currently on hold due to new EU customs policies. Navigator (30th Anniversary Edition) by Forma Tadre About Forma Tadre Forma Tadre began in 1986 as a three-piece band in Lower Saxony, Germany, with Andreas Meyer among its members. Meyer took the project’s name from a portmanteau of Tangerine Dream’s album “Force Majeure,” after Tangerine Dream’s “Phaedra” prompted him to buy his first synthesizer. The band played live and recorded the EP “Brightful Times” in 1987, produced by German producer Robert “Bobby” Giddens, who had also worked with DAF. Two of the three members subsequently left without recording further material. Meyer was the sole member of Forma Tadre by 1994. After the trio dissolved, Haujobb’s Björn Junemann encouraged Meyer to send demo tapes to record labels, which led Off Beat to sign him. In 1996, Meyer released “Navigator” as his first album under the Forma Tadre name, built partly from songs he had written separately from the band under the working title “P-Songs.” Around 1995, Meyer also worked with a female vocalist on a separate, classically-oriented project named Eisriesenkönig, which released a single track on Off Beat’s 1996 compilation “The O-Files.” After “Navigator,” Daniel Myer of Haujobb approached Meyer to collaborate, and the two formed Newt. The duo released two albums and a single between 1997 and 1999. Through the 1990s and 2000s, Meyer produced remixes for acts including Haujobb, La Floa Maldita, New Mind, Wumpscut and Assemblage 23. Forma Tadre’s second album, “Automate,” followed in 1998 and shifted toward a more ambient sound. After close to a decade of silence, Meyer returned Forma Tadre in 2008 with the 13-track album “The Music of Erich Zann,” inspired by H.P. Lovecraft’s short story of the same name. In 2019, “Brightful Times” was reissued as a hybrid vinyl-and-digital edition that added eight tracks recorded between 1987 and 1992 to the original four-track EP. In 2020, Forma Tadre released two archival anthologies. “Navigator Travelogue” collected remixes, singles, demos and unreleased tracks from 1994-1997, and “P-SongX, the hidden path” gathered personal recordings that predated “Navigator.” In 2021, Forma Tadre released “Geiger’s Day”, its first album issued on CD in 20 years. In 2025, the project followed with the digital archival compilation “Seven Century Factory”, which drew on demos and sketches recorded between 1997 and 2007. This reissue follows the 2019 vinyl-and-digital edition of “Brightful Times.” It extends Forma Tadre’s archival reissue campaign to “Navigator,” the project’s 1996 debut album.

items.body: Jesu Aparicio is a Spanish artist who sees himself first and foremost as a DJ, and only secondly as a producer. He has been active in the Spanish club scene for years and won me over this year with his album “Human Control”. The album was released on Jesu’s own label, Espacio Cielo, in collaboration with Mots Music. The name Parissior may not ring a bell for many, but I highly recommend this work to anyone with an interest in Dark-Techno and EBM. The album’s title and theme reflect the increasingly complex relationship between humans, technology, control, and the systems that shape our daily lives. By combining dark electronic sounds with an atmosphere that is both unsettling and intriguing, Parissior creates music that invites the listener to look beyond the surface. The album evokes the atmosphere and danceability of the 1990s Frankfurt Techno scene while adding a distinctly contemporary twist. For me, this record is one of this year’s best discoveries, making it the perfect time to meet the artist behind Parissior and talk to him about “Human Control”, his influences, and his approach to music. (Courtesy by Inferno Sound Diaries) Parissior interview Q: Could you give us some background on your musical activities, which apparently began quite some time ago as a DJ and eventually evolved into producing, leading to the Parissior project? Jesu: I began DJing professionally in my native Cantabria in 2001, playing Techno and House under my own name, ‘Jesu Aparicio’. In 2004, I moved to Salamanca, where I became a resident DJ at several venues, including Cubic Club, Submarino and Beatz. Those years were a major learning experience for me and gave me a much deeper understanding of the music industry. I eventually opened my own venue, Clavel Ocho, which featured an upstairs floor dedicated to Electronic music called Espacio Cielo – the name I would later revive for my record label. I started producing around 2004 and, over the years, explored many different styles and released music under several aliases. Altogether, I have released more than 600 tracks. I have always considered myself a DJ first and a producer second, although these days I actually spend more time producing music than performing as a DJ. Around 2011, I began to feel restricted by playing the same styles, so I created the Parissior alias as a way to broaden my musical horizons. It allowed me to explore funkier and more cosmic sounds, as well as Electro and Italo-Disco, eventually moving towards the EBM-influenced sound that has become an important part of the project’s identity. Q: Personally, I find it interesting that you moved into music production after starting out as a DJ – a role that naturally exposes you to a vast amount of music. This perhaps also helps explain the eclectic nature of your own work. What did your experience as a DJ bring to your approach to music-making, and what were some of your key influences and muses? Jesu: As a DJ, I have always been very eclectic and curious, and I have always enjoyed collecting music from a wide range of genres: ’80s music, Funk and Soul, Disco, Electro, House, Techno, Big Beat, Breaks… Salamanca had many clubs and bars, each with a very distinct musical identity, so playing there pushed you to dig deeper, discover new sounds and adapt to very different audiences. Being exposed to such a vast amount of music has undoubtedly had a major influence on the way I produce. You learn to recognize the formulas and ideas that make each genre work, and then reinterpret and adapt them to your own musical language. My influences have naturally evolved over the years, but I could never leave out Joy Division and New Order, Talking Heads, The Prodigy, The Chemical Brothers, Pet Shop Boys, Andrew Weatherall, Primal Scream or LCD Soundsystem, among many others. Q: You released the album “Human Control” this year, which, as I understand it, was not originally conceived as an album. How did it all come about, and how did the concept of “Human Control” take shape? Or did the concept emerge only afterwards, almost imposing itself on the music? Jesu: As you rightly say, the album was not initially planned as such. I had three tracks that I had deliberately held back from releasing on any label because they felt more personal, less focused on the dancefloor, and did not really fit with any of the EPs I had previously released. Almost without realizing it, I had incorporated phrases and messages into those tracks that shared a certain underlying theme: a defense of the analogue world and a critique of the artificiality and falsehood that often surround today’s digital culture and social media. Once I recognized that common thread, I decided to compose a series of new tracks around those original three and gradually shape the whole thing into an album. The first track I created with that intention was “Human Control.” It features a sample from a speech by Greta Thunberg at the UN Climate Action Summit, in which she delivers a passionate and somewhat dramatic rebuke to the world’s leaders. That track ultimately gave both the album and its central concept a clear identity. Q: What can you tell us about the writing and production process behind the album? What did you focus on most, and what were the different stages you went through to bring “Human Control” to completion? What tools and equipment did you work with, and what were the biggest challenges along the way? Jesu: One of the album’s defining features – and also its biggest challenge – was the decision to deliberately limit the amount of hardware and software I used on each track. I find that working within those kinds of restrictions forces me to be more creative, especially compared with having thousands of possibilities available in the form of plug-ins. My process was generally to choose a small palette of sound sources for each track, record the main parts, and then reshape and develop them through processing. For example, every synthesizer part on “True Connection” came from the Waldorf Pulse 2. Most of the basslines on the album were created with an analogue clone of the Roland SH-101, which I also used to design many of the drum sounds, while the Acid lines came from the Behringer TD-3. Another synthesizer that played a major role throughout the album was the Model D, and I also incorporated parts I had recorded years earlier with my Roland JX-3P. On the software side, I used Ableton’s stock plug-ins alongside Massive and Omnisphere. Massive was the only synthesizer used on “Human Control,” while Omnisphere appears more sparingly on some of the other tracks, mainly providing polyphonic textures. I also enjoy running synthesizers through effects pedals to create new tones and textures, while the vocals were processed using the Roland VT-4 and a variety of VST effects. Ultimately, the main focus was to get as much character and variety as possible from a relatively small and carefully chosen set of tools. Q: With this album, you explore themes such as digital identity, technology, artificial validation, and the relationship between humans and machines. Could you tell us a little more about these themes, and to what extent did they influence your decision to release the album on vinyl? To me, the physical format almost feels like a response to – or a reaction against – the increasingly digital nature of our lives. And if so, why vinyl rather than cassette? Jesu: That was exactly the idea. Releasing the album on vinyl was, in many ways, a reaction against the digitalisation of almost every aspect of our lives. Particularly since the pandemic, it often feels as though people’s lives have been reduced to the online alter egos they create on platforms such as Instagram – showing the world only what they want others to see and projecting lifestyles that they are not necessarily living in reality. Releasing a record on vinyl had also been unfinished business for me with Espacio Cielo, so my own album felt like the perfect opportunity to take that step. There was an economic reason as well: digital sales are falling every year as listening increasingly shifts towards streaming platforms such as Spotify, yet the royalties these services pay are extremely unfair. Sometimes you barely earn enough to buy a hamburger, which makes it very difficult for an independent label to remain financially sustainable. I also feel that digital music is more ephemeral. It disappears more quickly, becomes outdated faster and struggles to hold people’s attention. A vinyl record has a physical presence and a sense of permanence: people tend to spend more time with it, and it can remain part of their lives for years. In that sense, the format became a natural extension of the album’s concept. To be honest, I never seriously considered releasing it on cassette. It is a very nostalgic format, but I also think that very few people still own the equipment needed to play tapes. Of course, the same issue exists to some extent with vinyl, but many DJs have kept their Technics turntables, and the fact that the company has released new models such as the MK7 gives me some reason for optimism. Vinyl also has a much stronger connection to my own history as a DJ and to the culture surrounding this music. From now on, we plan to slow down the label’s digital release schedule and gradually release more records on vinyl. Who knows – perhaps in a few years we will release exclusively on vinyl. It is something I am seriously considering. Q: Where do you draw the line today between human control and the control we voluntarily surrender to technology? In what sense do you see the title and concept of “Human Control” as a warning, an observation, or perhaps even a personal confession? How do you see humans evolving alongside technological progress, and what role do you think the musician will play in that relationship? Jesu: That boundary is becoming increasingly blurred. There is no denying that we will benefit enormously from technological progress and that it will make many aspects of our lives easier. However, when it comes to art and culture, I believe we need to preserve certain principles and ensure that convenience and automation do not replace human intention, creativity and genuine expression. In that sense, “Human Control” is both an observation and a warning. Technology itself is not the enemy; the real question is how much control and creative autonomy we are willing to surrender to it. We should remain the ones making the decisions, with technology serving as a tool rather than dictating the creative process. At the same time, I think a counter-movement is beginning to emerge – one that will bring back a greater appreciation for craftsmanship, physical formats and live music. I am already seeing clubs programming exclusively live sets, as well as all-vinyl nights, which I find very encouraging. Perhaps the musician’s role in this new relationship will be precisely to preserve that human element: spontaneity, imperfection and a genuine connection with the audience. Q: Do you also perform your Parissior tracks live, or do they mainly form part of your DJ sets? How does that work in practice, and what can we expect from Parissior in the near future? Jesu: I have always considered myself more of a DJ than a producer, even though, since the pandemic, I have actually spent more time producing than performing. I love playing DJ sets, and while I already have enough of my own material prepared to develop a full live show, the right opportunity has not yet presented itself. For the moment, Parissior’s music therefore appears mainly within my DJ sets. I have performed hybrid sets using hardware, but fees are sometimes so limited today that paying for additional luggage to transport equipment becomes impractical. The same applies to vinyl: I play vinyl locally, but when I travel, I usually perform with CDJs for exactly the same reason. Because of my day job, I only play around five or six gigs a year, and promoters generally approach me to perform DJ sets. However, I would definitely like to explore the live format when the right opportunity and conditions come along. About Parissior Parissior is the alias of Spanish DJ and producer Jesu Aparicio. He began DJing professionally in his native Cantabria in 2001 under his own name, playing Techno and House. In 2004 he moved to Salamanca, where he became a resident DJ at venues including Cubic Club, Submarino and Beatz, and later opened his own venue, Clavel Ocho, whose upstairs floor, Espacio Cielo, was dedicated to electronic music. He started producing around 2004 and has released more than 600 tracks under various aliases. He created the Parissior alias in 2011 to explore Electro, Italo-Disco and EBM-influenced sounds beyond his earlier productions. Parissior has released singles and EPs since at least 2016, including “Could I Drown In Your Desire” and “Dance To The Groove” (Spa In Disco), followed by “Let Them Dance” (Hot Digits Music, 2017) and further EPs and compilation appearances for Golden Soul Records. From “Back To Earth” (2020) onward he has worked mainly through Espacio Cielo, the label he revived from his former venue’s name, releasing further singles, EPs and compilation tracks including “Battle Cry” (2021), “Raver In The Booth” and “Full of Stars” (2023), and the Skylax release “Antennae” (2024). “Human Control”, Parissior’s first full-length album, was released on Espacio Cielo in collaboration with Mots Music. Side-Line reviewed the album in September 2026, describing it as a mix of Dark-Techno and EBM. This interview follows that review.

items.body: Hermidgets, the anonymous Italian dark synthpop project, has released “Like Moths” alongside an official video. The single is out now through Bandcamp and is the fourth preview of Hermidgets’ third album, expected in early 2027. “Like Moths” was mixed by Matteo Sandri and mastered by Giovanni Versari. A bass-heavy opening gives way to rhythmic, buzzing synthesizers, with Hermidgets’ baritone vocal set against a danceable groove and a bright, wiry synth line that recurs through the track. The lyrics follow two people drawn into a relationship whose destructive pull has become part of its appeal, turning surrender into something close to devotional: “Learn how to pray for the pleasure of having nothing.” The video, directed around a concept developed independently of the song, was inspired by French artist Olivier de Sagazan. Shot in black and white, it isolates Hermidgets’ head and shoulders as white modeling clay obscures and distorts his features throughout the performance, with black pigment introduced later in the video. The project keeps its members unidentified, and the clay imagery extends that approach by withholding a clear view of the performer’s face. Like Moths by Hermidgets About Hermidgets Hermidgets is an Italian electronic project that does not identify its members, combining distorted synthpop and darkwave songwriting with self-produced visuals. The debut album, “The Mire,” was released in November 2020 and included the songs “This Is Over” and “Nothing’s Perfect.” The singles “A Flaw” and “Perks” followed in 2021, and “Meaninglessness” and “We Tend to Disappear” appeared on the mini-album “NIHIL” in June 2024, recorded with a limited setup of two analog synthesizers, drum samples and voice. Hermidgets began previewing a third album with the single “Fall Apart” in July 2025, followed by “Sundown” in December 2025 and “Could I Be Better” in March 2026, a song that revisits “Could Be Better” from the 2020 debut. “Like Moths,” released in September 2026, is the fourth single from that album cycle, with the full album expected in early 2027.

items.body: Mass Minor, the Austin, Texas-based darkwave and electronic rock project of Andrew J. Martin Jr., released the single “Get Up” on 2 October 2026 via Metropolis Records. Get Up by Mass Minor “This song is a conversation with God at 169 BPM about sin, money, mortality and the things we sacrifice our lives to,” Martin says of the track. “It comes from this idea of asking God to save us from problems we created ourselves. Maybe it’s not God’s job to save us. Maybe we need to fix our own shit. You’re the one holding the light. Get up.” A music video for “Get Up”, directed by Teresa Jolie and edited by Beau Loy, accompanies the release. “Get Up” follows “Nowhere Now”, issued as a single in late July. Both songs are set to appear on a new Mass Minor album, “Beyond The Edge Of Reason”, due out in late February 2027 on Metropolis Records. About Mass Minor Mass Minor is the Austin, Texas-based project of Andrew J. Martin Jr., who blends atmospheric synths and driving guitars with post-punk, synth-pop and alternative rock influences. Martin self-released the project’s debut album, “Become Each Other”, in 2020, followed by a run of singles later collected on EPs. The project built a presence in the dark alternative scene through radio support, multiple SXSW appearances and shows alongside acts including Twin Tribes, Ultra Sunn, TRAITRS, Vision Video, Urban Heat and Sacred Skin. Mass Minor signed to Metropolis Records and released the single “Nowhere Now” in July 2026, followed by “Get Up” on 2 October 2026. Both tracks lead into the project’s next album, “Beyond The Edge Of Reason”, due in late February 2027.

items.body: Susanne Jonsson and Jan Strandqvist of the Swedish band Red Mecca have returned after a hiatus. Their time away, however, was marked by intense and deeply painful experiences: Susanne’s sister was murdered and her relationship fell apart, while Jan struggled with addiction. Sometimes, nothing seems better than returning to creative expression—in their case, by making a new album. This record clearly holds great significance for them, even though the music remains true to Red Mecca’s signature sound and style. It is a polished album, balancing understated, sensitive, and refined tracks with a somewhat ‘harder’ Synth-Pop style. The songs are expertly crafted and beautifully sung by Susanne Jonsson, a vocalist who has nothing left to prove. Personally, I prefer their Electro-Pop style—which occasionally hints at EBM elements—as it really showcases their talent for creating great music. While some tracks may lack a definitive climax, I believe the choice to create a more restrained work was deliberate. This may not be my favorite album by the duo, but it stands as a significant and healing production in their career. (Rating:7½). Listen to “I’m On The Outside”: I’m On The Outside by Red Mecca About Red Mecca Red Mecca was set up by Jan Strandqvist, originally with vocalist Frida Madeleine, who left after four albums and was replaced by Susanne Jonsson. The Swedish duo released “Truth” in 2019, followed by the albums “Away” (2021) and “Stay” (2023), all on Massproduktion. Strandqvist discussed the band’s history, including a 2016 Swedish Manifest Award win and a soundtrack placement on “Killing Eve”, in a 2021 Side-Line Click Interview.
